papers.title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
papers.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.

papers.title: Copying versus self-construction in cellular automata: an algorithmic-information approach to self-reproduction
papers.abstract: What distinguishes an object that reproduces itself from one that is merely copied by its environment? We propose an answer based on algorithmic information and interventions, in cellular automata. Copies of an object are identified by the algorithmic information they share with it. Its code and its machine are identified by perturbations: changes to the code are inherited by the offspring, changes to the machine are not, since the offspring's machine is rebuilt from the code. An object is a self-reproducer if it proliferates, admits such a decomposition, its machine can be decoded from its code, and removing the machine stops the code from being copied. The definition uses only counts, interventions and upper bounds on information, so it is not undermined by exhaustive search. We prove that it excludes trivial "infection" dynamics and rules that copy every pattern, and reduce the claim that it includes the construction of von Neumann and Burks, but not its constituents, to explicit hypotheses. We measure the amount of self-reproduction by the length of the shortest proof, in a fixed formal theory, that some machinery can stand in for the object's machine; its lower bounds are decidable and immune to search. In an abstract model of reproduction we show that both ingredients are necessary: no criterion computed from the observed run alone distinguishes a machine built from its description from one that is copied, and criteria that ignore the dynamical law attribute to the object information the law supplies. We also show that conditional Kolmogorov complexity is, up to logarithmic terms, the only effective notion of determination compatible with counting and with charging re-encodings by their description length. Finally, we show that separate weak dependence of a function on its arguments implies joint weak dependence only non-effectively, with a loss governed by the halting problem.

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Learning of Random Automata from One Label per Word
papers.abstract: We study a binary deterministic finite automaton whose $2n$ transitions are chosen independently and uniformly from its $n$ states. The learner observes independent uniform words of length $m$, each labeled with a single bit indicating acceptance. For every fixed $\beta>0$ we give a polynomial-time algorithm that works outside a set of transition tables of probability $o(n^{-\beta})$. On each remaining table, for any start state and accepting set, the predictor has error at most $\epsilon$ on fresh uniform words of length $m$ with probability at least $1-\gamma$ over the training sample and the learner's random choices. Its sample size and running time are polynomial in $n$, $m$, $1/\epsilon$ and $\log(2/\gamma)$, with degree depending only on $\beta$. Although each word reveals only one output, comparing label moments at two consecutive history lengths lets us estimate the expected product of the signed outputs of two continuations from the same hidden state. We also refute Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times. For two distinct states fixed before the table is drawn and every fixed $c>0$, the fraction of words of length $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ that send them to different states converges in probability to $e^{-c}$. On a typical table, driving this fraction down to $1/n$ takes asymptotically $n\log n$ letters. Selected proof steps are formalized in Lean.

papers.title: Subword enumeration up to stack-sorting equivalence
papers.abstract: Defant and Kravitz introduced generalizations of West's stack-sorting map $s$ from permutations to finite words. This raises questions as to how such generalizations could be applied in the field of combinatorics on words. The Defant-Kravitz generalizations of $s$ depend on how repeated occurrences of the same character within a word may be repositioned, according to their $\textsf{tortoise}$ and $\textsf{hare}$ operations. As demonstrated in this paper, these operations provide a natural way of extending abelian complexity functions for infinite sequences, in a way that gives light to structural properties associated with infinite words. We apply these new ideas to two famous infinite words: the paperfolding word and the Thue-Morse word. In the case of the Thue-Morse word, we discover an interesting connection to the previous work of several authors, such as de Luca and Varricchio, on the ``special'' factors of the Thue-Morse word. This may be seen as providing a basis for a new and interdisciplinary area linking the combinatorics about the stack-sorting of permutations with the field of combinatorics on words.

papers.title: BEAVER: An Efficient Deterministic LLM Verifier
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) transition from research prototypes to production systems, practitioners need reliable ways to verify model outputs before they are deployed. While sampling-based estimates provide an ad-hoc intuition of model behavior, they offer no sound guarantees. We present BEAVER, the first practical framework for computing deterministic, sound bounds on the probability that an LLM's response to a prompt satisfies a property. Given a prompt and an oracle, BEAVER systematically explores the model's output distribution using a *token trie* and a *frontier*, maintaining provably sound bounds at every iteration. We formalize the LLM verification problem, prove that BEAVER's bounds are sound and that its selection strategy Max-$\mu$ is optimal for verification upto any tolerance. On 3 important safety tasks across 5 popular LLMs, BEAVER certifies up to $7.6\times$ more prompts as risky than a sampling-based verifier while using fewer forward passes, and its per-prompt bounds extend to statistical certificates over distributions of prompts.

papers.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^2$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
papers.abstract: Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{2-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{2k-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size. Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.
